name: THE SHOULD I SAUTEE OR SHOULD I MANGO BURGER (comes with sauteed onions and mango salsa)

recipe.history:
The mango — Mangifera indica — is arguably the most beloved fruit on earth by volume of human devotion, consumed by more people in more countries than any other fruit except the banana. Its origins are in the tropical forests of South and Southeast Asia, with genetic evidence suggesting that mango cultivation began in the northeastern regions of India and Myanmar approximately four thousand years ago. Sanskrit literature references mangoes as far back as 2000 BCE, and the fruit is so woven into Hindu religious and cultural life that the mango tree is considered sacred, its leaves hung at doorways during festivals, its fruit offered to the gods. From India, the mango spread across trade routes to East Africa and the Persian Gulf by the tenth century CE, and Portuguese traders carried it to West Africa and Brazil in the sixteenth century, from which it spread across the Caribbean and into Latin America. The extraordinary diversity of mango varieties — there are over a thousand distinct cultivars, from the Alphonso of Maharashtra to the Ataulfo of Chiapas to the Kent of Florida — reflects millennia of cultivation across vastly different climates and cultures, each community developing its own preferred expression of the fruit's possibilities.

Mango salsa entered American popular cuisine through the borderlands of the American Southwest and through the Caribbean-influenced cooking of Florida and the Gulf Coast, where proximity to Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean islands created a natural culinary corridor. By the 1980s and 1990s, mango salsa had moved from regional specialty to mainstream grocery store shelf, riding the broader wave of American interest in tropical flavors. Its application to burgers was a natural evolution — the mango's combination of sweetness, acidity, and a hint of resinous perfume makes it one of the most effective foils for rich, fatty beef, cutting through the heaviness of the patty in the same way a well-made chimichurri or giardiniera does, but with a tropical brightness uniquely its own. Sautéed onions alongside mango salsa create a burger of complementary contrasts: the deep, savory sweetness of slow-cooked allium against the bright, raw sweetness of fresh mango.

I ate my first mango cut from a tree standing in someone's backyard in Florida when I was in my early twenties, and it tasted so little like the mangoes I had eaten from grocery stores in the North that I asked what kind of fruit it was. The answer — 'a mango, but an actual one' — felt like an accusation that I had been living a diminished life, which was accurate. Ever since, I have been somewhat obsessive about sourcing the best available mangoes for cooking: the flat Ataulfo when I can find them, which are creamier and less fibrous than the Tommy Atkins variety that dominates American grocery stores, or whatever a good farmer's market has that came off the tree recently. A mango salsa made with a genuinely ripe fruit is a completely different object from one made with a hard, underripe supermarket mango, and the difference matters on this burger.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — creates a specific thermal environment that makes the mango salsa work at its highest possible level. A medium-rare patty is warm enough to slightly perfume the cold salsa laid over it, releasing additional aromatic volatiles from the mango, lime, and cilantro, without cooking them and destroying their freshness. The pink juices from the patty flow down through the sautéed onions and mango alike, carrying beef flavor into the fruit and creating a bridge between savory and sweet that is one of the great pleasures of this burger. A well-done patty in this context is simply a dry platform under beautiful fruit — inert, desiccated, irrelevant. Medium rare makes the beef a participant. Medium rare is the only correct answer.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened and cubed
2 large ripe Ataulfo or Tommy Atkins mangoes, peeled and diced into 1/4-inch pieces (about 2 cups)
1 jalapeño, seeds removed for less heat, finely minced
3 large sweet onions (Vidalia or Walla Walla), halved and thinly sliced
2 chipotle peppers in adobo sauce, minced to a paste
1 teaspoon adobo sauce from the can
1 clove garlic, minced to a paste
6 slices pepper jack cheese (about 1 oz each)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE: Combine warm milk, warm water, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.

2. Add flour, remaining sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes, then medium 6 minutes. Add butter one cube at a time on medium speed over 8 to 10 minutes. Increase to medium-high and mix 6 to 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight (8 to 12 hours).
4. Next day, divide dough into 6 equal portions. Shape into tight round balls. Proof on parchment-lined baking sheet, covered, 2 to 3 hours until puffed.
5. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a wire rack.

6. MAKE THE MANGO SALSA: Combine diced mango, red onion, jalapeño, and cilantro in a bowl. Add lime juice, lime zest, honey, cumin, salt, and cayenne. Toss gently to combine. Taste and adjust lime, salt, and heat. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes to allow flavors to meld. Bring to room temperature before serving.

7. MAKE THE SAUTÉED ONIONS: Melt butter with oil in a wide heavy skillet over medium heat. Add onions and salt. Cook, stirring every 5 minutes, for 30 to 40 minutes until deeply golden and soft. These are sautéed onions — slightly less deeply caramelized than a long slow caramel — with some texture remaining. Add thyme and apple cider vinegar in the last 5 minutes. Stir to incorporate. Set aside and keep warm.

8. MAKE THE CHIPOTLE-LIME AIOLI: Whisk egg yolks, mustard, and garlic paste in a medium bowl. Stream in neutral oil very slowly while whisking constantly until the emulsion forms and thickens. Whisk in lime juice and zest. Stir in chipotle paste and adobo sauce. Add honey. Season with kosher salt. Refrigerate until needed.
9. SHRED THE CABBAGE SLAW: Toss shredded cabbage with lime juice, olive oil, and a pinch of salt just before assembly. Set aside.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground sirloin. Season with salt, pepper, garlic powder, and smoked paprika. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
11. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side until a deep brown crust forms.

12. Flip once. Lay a slice of pepper jack cheese over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
13. TOAST THE BUNS: Split buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread chipotle-lime aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place the dressed cabbage slaw on the bottom bun. Add the rested, cheese-topped patty.
15. Spoon sautéed onions over the patty. Spoon mango salsa generously over and around the onions, allowing it to tumble over the sides.
16. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately with extra mango salsa on the side.
